title: Design an Elevator System (OOD)
oneLiner: N floors, M cars: which car answers a call, what order a car stops in, and how fire mode fits in later.
keyTakeaway: Split the problem in two: a dispatch strategy decides which car takes a hall call, and each car orders its own stops with a sweep (keep going while there are stops ahead, then reverse). Feed every button press through one control loop so car state has a single writer.
explanation:
Same format as the parking lot: write your answer for each of the seven stages first, then compare it with the model answer and tick what you covered. See the parking lot walk-through for what an OOD round is and how it's graded.

What's specific to the elevator. Most of the difficulty is behaviour over time rather than data, so the interviewer wants to see the algorithm as code: how a car keeps its stops, how it moves one floor, when it reverses or goes idle. Candidates often merge two different decisions, which car answers a floor's call and in what order one car visits its stops, into one tangled method. Keeping them apart is the main design point, and it's what makes a new dispatch policy (zoning, rush hour, destination dispatch) a single new class.

Expect the State pattern question: is the car's direction a state machine? For direction alone an enum is enough; for modes that change how the car reacts to everything (fire service, maintenance, overload) separate mode classes start to pay. Have a view either way and say what would change your mind. Concurrency comes up too: buttons are pressed from many places at once, and the simplest correct answer is a queue in front of one control loop rather than locks inside every car.
